title: Integrated survey area plan certification and acceptance
mainQuestion: How do certification, Director acceptance, title effect, and geographic scope work for a survey plan in an integrated survey area?
studySummary: For plans prepared under section 7 in integrated survey areas, a surveyor may certify correctness only when the plan represents a survey carried out by the surveyor or under the surveyor's personal supervision or direction and the survey standard follows the regulations. The Director of Surveys cannot accept an uncertified plan, acceptance is not an adjudication on title, and the section applies only to integrated survey areas constituted under section 5.

objectives.objective: Recall when a surveyor may certify correctness of a plan prepared under section 7.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What conditions must be met before the surveyor certifies correctness of a subdivision or other plan prepared under section 7?
objectives.studyAnswer: The plan must represent a survey carried out by the surveyor or under the surveyor's personal supervision or direction, and the standard of survey employed must be in accordance with the regulations.

evidence.evidenceText: When a surveyor prepares a subdivision or other plan under section 7, he or she shall not certify to the correctness of the plan unless it represents a survey carried out by the surveyor or under his or her personal supervision or direction, and the standard of survey employed is in accordance with the regulations.

objectives.objective: Recall the Director of Surveys acceptance limit for uncertified plans.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What is the Director of Surveys prohibited from accepting if surveyor certification is missing?
objectives.studyAnswer: Unless a surveyor has certified the correctness of a plan, the Director of Surveys shall not accept it.

evidence.evidenceText: Unless a surveyor has certified to the correctness of a plan, the Director of Surveys shall not accept it.

objectives.objective: Recall the title effect of Director acceptance.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What does Director of Surveys acceptance of a plan not decide?
objectives.studyAnswer: When the Director of Surveys accepts a plan, that acceptance does not constitute an adjudication on title.

evidence.evidenceText: When the Director of Surveys accepts a plan, the acceptance does not constitute an adjudication on title.

objectives.objective: Recall the geographic scope of section 8.
objectives.guidedQuestion: Where does the section 8 survey plan rule apply?
objectives.studyAnswer: Section 8 applies only to integrated survey areas as constituted under section 5.

evidence.evidenceText: This section applies to only integrated survey areas as constituted under section 5.

title: Planning-control regulation subjects under section 125(1)
mainQuestion: Which physical planning, site-use, advertising, extraction, and subdivision subjects may be regulated under section 125(1)?
studySummary: Section 125(1) permits regulations on selected planning-control subjects, including building setbacks from street boundaries, mobile home parks and sites, automotive service uses, public advertising signs and billboards, commercial excavation of deposits, and the subdividing of land.

objectives.objective: Recall the setback regulation power.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What setback subject may regulations govern for buildings and structures?
objectives.studyAnswer: Regulations may govern the setting back of buildings and structures from the boundaries of streets or classes of streets.

evidence.evidenceText: governing the setting back of buildings and structures from the boundaries of streets or classes of streets

objectives.objective: Recall the site and automotive-use subjects that may be regulated.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What mobile home park and automotive service subjects may regulations prescribe or approve?
objectives.studyAnswer: Regulations may prescribe the location, layout, equipment, standards, licensing, site standards, and operator fees for mobile home parks, and may prescribe the location and dimensions of service stations, gas bars, car washes, and automotive repair garages while approving construction standards.

objectives.objective: Recall sign, excavation, and subdivision regulation subjects.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What public advertising, excavation, and subdivision subjects are included in the listed regulation powers?
objectives.studyAnswer: Regulations may address the location, dimensions, purposes, licensing, construction standards, and fees for public advertising signs and billboards; govern excavation of listed deposits for sale or other commercial use; and respect the subdividing of land.

title: Development approval and building-work regulation powers
mainQuestion: How may section 125(1) regulations address building work, development approvals, inspection fees, and related approval controls?
studySummary: The regulation power includes building-work controls for buildings and structures, including standards and prohibitions on work that violates standards. It also includes development approval processes, application and approval terms, fees for applications, approvals, and building inspection services, approval information for assessment purposes, and a wiring-permit prohibition tied to delivery of a development approval copy.

objectives.objective: Recall the building-work subjects that may be regulated.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What building and structure work may regulations address under paragraph 125(1)(g)?
objectives.studyAnswer: Regulations may respect the building, dimensions, locating or relocating, demolishing, altering, structurally altering, repairing, replacing, or combined work on buildings and structures, including standards for the work and prohibiting work that violates the standards.

evidence.evidenceText: respecting the building, dimensions, locating or relocating, demolishing, altering, structurally altering, repairing or replacing, or a combination of the work, of buildings and structures, including, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, standards for the work and the prohibiting of the undertaking or continuing of the work in violation of the standards

objectives.objective: Recall the development approval process and terms regulation power.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What parts of development approval administration may regulations cover?
objectives.studyAnswer: Regulations may cover development approval applications, granting, suspending, reinstating and revoking approvals, forms, terms and conditions on applications and approval decisions, terms and conditions on granted approvals, and related information provided to the Executive Director of Assessment and its use.

evidence.evidenceText: respecting development approvals, including, without limitation, (i) the process with respect to applications for approvals and with respect to granting, suspending, reinstating and revoking approvals, including forms, (ii) the terms and conditions on applications for approvals and on suspending, reinstating and revoking approvals, (iii) the terms and conditions on granting approvals, (iv) the fees for applications, approvals and for building inspection services, (v) the provision of information with respect to approvals to the Executive Director of Assessment under the Assessment Act and the use to be made of the information

objectives.objective: Recall the wiring-permit prohibition tied to development approval.
objectives.guidedQuestion: When may a regulation prohibit issuing an electrical wiring permit for a development?
objectives.studyAnswer: In part of an area where a paragraph (g) or (h) regulation is in effect, a regulation may prohibit issuing a wiring permit for a development unless the wiring-permit applicant delivers a copy of the development approval.

evidence.evidenceText: in a part of an area in which a regulation under paragraph (g) or (h) is in effect, prohibiting the issue of a wiring permit under the Electrical Installation and Inspection Act in respect of a development unless the applicant for the wiring permit delivers a copy of the approval for the development

title: Supporting rules for section 125 planning and development regulations
mainQuestion: What supporting fee, application, delegation, subdivision, consultation, summary, and filing rules surround section 125 regulations?
studySummary: Subsections 125(2) through 125(16) cover multiple operational rules: where certain fees go, how regulations may be applied to areas and local governments, how land-use policy regulations prevail, how development-officer and regional-service-commission powers operate, how subdivision public-purpose land and money are handled, what consultation or preliminary procedure is required before making regulations, when a written summary may stand in for making a proposed rural plan or amendment available, and where regulations must be filed. Because those topics are too varied for one durable recall unit, this proposal is marked for map revision.

objectives.objective: Recall fee treatment and area-effect rules for regulations under section 125.
objectives.guidedQuestion: How do subsections 125(2) through 125(8) deal with prescribed fees, designated areas, local effectiveness, inconsistency, rural-plan consistency, and development-officer status?
objectives.studyAnswer: A paragraph (1)(h) fee is paid to the regional service commission and credited to land use planning service delivery. The Lieutenant-Governor in Council may designate areas for regulation application, subject to limits, and subdivision regulations may apply throughout the Province except excluded areas. The subsections also state local effectiveness limits, paragraph (1)(j) precedence over inconsistent instruments except a statement-of-public-interest regulation, rural-plan consistency, and development-officer status.

evidence.evidenceText: If a fee is prescribed under paragraph (1)(h), the fee shall be paid, despite the Financial Administration Act, to the regional service commission and shall be credited to the cost of the delivery of the land use planning service under subsection 161(4) of the Local Governance Act.

Subject to subsections (4) and (7), the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may (a) except in the case of a rural plan under section 51, designate an area or areas for the purpose of the application of a regulation under this section, thereby restricting, subject to paragraph (b), the application of the regulation accordingly, and (b) with respect to a subdivision regulation, provide that the regulation applies throughout the Province exclusive of those areas identified in the regulation as not being subject to the regulation.

A regulation under this section (a) subject to paragraph (b), is not effective in a municipality; (b) if made under paragraph (1)(a) or (f), is effective in a village that is within an area in which it applies and (i) in the case of a regulation under paragraph (1)(a), no zoning by-law or zoning provisions in a rural plan under section 33 are in effect in the village, or (ii) in the case of a regulation under paragraph (1)(f), no subdivision by-law is in effect in the village; and (c) is not effective in a rural community that has a by-law in effect respecting the same matter as the regulation.
Despite subsection (4), a regulation under paragraph (1)(j) is effective in a local government or local service district specified in the regulation.

Despite any other provision in this Act, if there is an inconsistency between a regulation under paragraph (1)(j) and a regional land use plan, rural plan, municipal plan or by-law or regulation under this Act, except a regulation establishing a statement of public interest, the regulation under paragraph (1)(j) prevails.

With respect to a regulation made under this section applicable in an area designated under subsection (3) or paragraph 52(1)(a), the regulation shall be consistent with a rural plan, if any, in effect in the area.

If a regulation under this section is in effect, the planning director as defined in the Regional Services Delivery Act is the development officer and the powers vested in a regional service commission under paragraph (9)(a) or (e), (10)(b) or (11)(b) shall be deemed to be vested in the regional service commission.

objectives.objective: Recall zoning regulation and rural-plan powers under subsection 125(9).
objectives.guidedQuestion: What kinds of powers may be vested or adapted for a zoning regulation or zoning provisions in a rural plan under section 125?
objectives.studyAnswer: Subsection 125(9) allows listed section 53 powers and functions, powers respecting particular uses, a Minister letter for one section 53 requirement, possible regional service commission powers, Consolidated Fund treatment and possible return of a fee, deemed vesting of certain proposed-use and variance powers, and Minister orders or agreements for rezoning applications with section 59 applying with necessary modifications.

evidence.evidenceText: 125(9)With respect to a zoning regulation or to zoning provisions in a rural plan under this section (a) the powers and functions referred to in paragraphs 53(2)(g), (g.1) and (h) or paragraph 53(3)(c), with respect to particular uses of land, may be vested in a regional service commission, (b) if the power referred to in subparagraph 53(2)(i)(ii) is provided for in the regulation, a letter from the Minister shall satisfy the requirement of clause 53(2)(i)(ii)(C), (c) the power referred to in paragraph 53(2)(j) may be vested in a regional service commission and, if it is, subsection 53(9) applies with the necessary modifications to the regulation, (d) if a fee referred to in paragraph 53(2)(l) is provided for in the regulation, it shall be paid into the Consolidated Fund, but may be returned in whole or in part on the advice of the Minister, (e) the powers referred to in sections 55 and 56 with respect to certain proposed uses and variances shall be deemed to be vested in the relevant regional service commission or development officer, as the case may be, and (f) if a person applies to the Minister to have an area of land re-zoned to permit the carrying out of a specific proposal, (i) the Minister, in relation to the application, may make an order or enter into an agreement with the person, and (ii) the provisions of section 59 with respect to a resolution or agreement under that section apply with the necessary modifications to an order or agreement made under this section.

objectives.objective: Recall subdivision public-purpose land, money, and related procedure rules.
objectives.guidedQuestion: How do subsections 125(10) through 125(13) deal with subdivision public-purpose land, money in lieu, approval powers, and later treatment of land or money?
objectives.studyAnswer: A subdivision regulation may provide for public-purpose land on a subdivision plan and vesting in the Crown on filing, money in lieu at the Minister's discretion, regional service commission powers about access and plan approval, tentative-plan fees, street-name approval, and added exemptions. Related subsections apply subdivision by-law, variance, and plan rules with modifications, and govern later public-purpose use, conveyance, special-account, investment, and local-government transfer treatment for the land or money.

evidence.evidenceText: 125(10)A subdivision regulation under this section may (a) subject to subsections (12) and (13), provide for (i) the setting aside of land for public purposes at a location as may be approved by the Minister after consultation with the regional service commission, the indicating of the land on a subdivision plan and the vesting of the land in the Crown on the filing of the subdivision plan in the land registration office, and (ii) the paying, at the discretion of the Minister, of money in lieu of land mentioned in subparagraph (i), (b) vest in a regional service commission the power referred to in paragraph 75(1)(c) with respect to access, (c) vest in a regional service commission the power referred to in paragraph 75(1)(k) with respect to approval of a subdivision plan, (d) prescribe the fee to be paid for the approval of a tentative plan, including prescribing different fees for the approval of tentative plans for type 1 subdivisions and type 2 subdivisions, (e) provide that the naming of streets in subdivisions is subject to the approval of the regional service commission, and (f) add to the list of exemptions referred to in subsection 80(1) with respect to land in the area to which the regulation applies.

125(11)If a subdivision regulation under this section is in effect, (a) the provisions of section 77 with respect to a subdivision by-law apply with the necessary modifications to the regulation, except if a plan involves the setting aside of land for public purposes, in which case the plan shall not be approved unless (i) the location of the land has been recommended by the regional service commission, and (ii) the plan has been approved and signed by the Minister, (b) the powers mentioned in section 78 with respect to variance are vested in the regional service commission or development officer, as the case may be, and (c) sections 79 and 80 apply with the necessary modifications to the regulation.

125(12)Land vested in the Crown under this section shall be held undeveloped or developed for public purposes and may, if subsequently included within the boundaries of a local government, be conveyed to the local government and the land shall be subject to all provisions of this Act affecting land for public purposes vested in a local government under this Act.

125(13)All money received by the Minister in lieu of land for public purposes or realized by the Minister on the sale of the land is to be paid into a special account, and the money in that account is to be expended by the Minister for acquiring or developing land for public purposes and for no other purpose, and (a) pending the expenditure the money shall be invested and the earnings derived from the investments paid into the special account, and (b) if a subdivision in respect of which money has been received is subsequently included within the boundaries of a local government, the portion of the money that remains unexpended, together with any increments that have accrued under paragraph (a), is to be paid to the local government of which the subdivision becomes a part, and is to be treated by the local government in the same manner as money received for a public purpose under a subdivision by-law.

objectives.objective: Recall pre-making consultation and summary rules for section 125 regulations.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What must the Minister do before making a section 125 regulation, and when may a written summary satisfy the public-consideration step?
objectives.studyAnswer: Before making a regulation, the Minister must request views from the regional service commission if the regulation would affect a region, request views from an advisory committee for a section 51 regulation affecting a rural district that has one, and follow the section 111 preliminary by-law procedure with necessary modifications except for paragraph (1)(a), (b), (f), or (g) regulations. For a zoning regulation under subsection (1) or a rural plan under section 51, a written summary may be made available for public consideration instead of the proposed rural plan or amendment.

evidence.evidenceText: 125(14)Before making a regulation under this section, the Minister shall (a) if the regulation would have effect in a region, request the regional service commission to give its views on the regulation, (b) if the regulation is to be made under section 51 and would have effect in a rural district that has an advisory committee, request the advisory committee to give its views on the regulation, and (c) follow, with the necessary modifications, the procedure preliminary to the making of a by-law under section 111, except if the regulation is to be made under paragraph (1)(a), (b), (f) or (g).

125(15)Despite paragraph (14)(c), with respect to a zoning regulation under subsection (1) or a rural plan under section 51, the provisions of section 111 shall not be read as requiring the Minister to make available for public consideration the proposed rural plan or amendment if the Minister makes available for public consideration a written summary of the proposed rural plan or amendment.

objectives.objective: Recall filing of section 125 regulations and the effect of filing on commencement.
objectives.guidedQuestion: Where must the Director file section 125 regulations, and is filing required before they come into force?
objectives.studyAnswer: The Director must file a copy of each section 125 regulation in the land registration office for every county where affected land is situated, but that filing is not a condition precedent to the regulation coming into force.

evidence.evidenceText: The Director shall file a copy of each regulation made under this section in the land registration office for every county in which any land affected by the regulation is situated, but the filing shall not be a condition precedent to the coming into force of the regulation.

title: Instrument receipt, examination, acceptance, and rejection
mainQuestion: What steps and rejection powers govern an instrument received for filing or registration at a land titles office?
studySummary: The registrar assigns each received instrument a registration number, date, and time and records those details in the instrument record. The instrument is then examined, acceptance is recorded subject to the rejection power, accepted instruments are registered, and the registrar may refuse or reject instruments for unpaid fees or listed defects such as wrong district, parcel-identifier problems, incompleteness, improper form, or non-compliance with the Community Planning Act if applicable.

objectives.objective: Recall the first record-entry step for a received instrument.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What must the registrar assign and record when an instrument is received for filing or registration?
objectives.studyAnswer: The registrar shall assign a registration number, date, and time to every instrument received at the land titles office for filing or registration, and shall enter a record of the instrument, date, time, and number in the instrument record.

evidence.evidenceText: The registrar shall assign a registration number, date and time to every instrument received at the land titles office for filing or registration and shall enter a record of the instrument, date, time and number in the instrument record.

objectives.objective: Recall examination, acceptance record, and registration after acceptance.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What happens after an instrument is entered in the instrument record and accepted for registration?
objectives.studyAnswer: The instrument is examined, and subject to subsection 18(4), a record of its acceptance for filing or registration is entered in the instrument record. When accepted for registration under subsection 18(2), it shall be registered.

evidence.evidenceText: The instrument shall then be examined and, subject to subsection (4), a record of the acceptance of the instrument for filing or registration shall be entered in the instrument record.
When an instrument is accepted for registration pursuant to subsection (2), it shall be registered.

objectives.objective: Recall the registrar's grounds for refusing, filing, registering, or rejecting an instrument.
objectives.guidedQuestion: On what grounds may the registrar refuse to file or register and reject an instrument?
objectives.studyAnswer: The registrar may refuse to file or register and may reject an instrument if the appropriate fee has not been paid, or if the instrument does not relate to land in the registrar's district, lacks the approved parcel identifier or is otherwise incomplete, uses a retired parcel identifier or adds a land description in addition to the approved parcel identifier, is not in proper form or fit for filing or registration, or does not comply with the Community Planning Act if applicable.

evidence.evidenceText: 18(4)Notwithstanding anything in this or any other enactment, the registrar may refuse to file or register and may reject an instrument where the appropriate fee has not been paid therefor or where the instrument (a) does not relate to land situated in his district; (b) does not describe the land to which it relates by its approved parcel identifier, or is otherwise incomplete; (b.1) describes the land (i) by reference to a parcel identifier that has been marked as retired by the registrar, or (ii) by a description of the land in addition to a reference to its approved parcel identifier; (c) is not in proper form or fit for filing or registration; or (d) does not comply with the Community Planning Act, if applicable.

title: Certificates and notices after land titles registration actions
mainQuestion: What certificate, notice, statutory-application, and parcel-identifier steps follow specified land titles registration actions?
studySummary: When the registrar performs specified registration actions involving land, ownership, severance, consolidation, or transfers, the registrar cancels any existing certificate of registered ownership and issues a new certificate to the appropriate person, including separate certificates for subdivision lots, blocks, or parcels. For titles registered under orders or for previously unregistered land under section 23, the registrar issues and records a Registry Act notice, after which the title and related instruments or documents are dealt with under the Land Titles Act. Each parcel whose title is registered under the Act must be identified by its approved parcel identifier in the title register.

objectives.objective: Recall certificate cancellation and issuance when specified registration actions occur.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What must the registrar do with certificates of registered ownership when required to register land, ownership, severance, consolidation, or a transfer?
objectives.studyAnswer: The registrar shall cancel any certificate of registered ownership for the land and issue a certificate of registered ownership to the owner, surviving owner, personal representative, agent, or trustee as the case may be; for a subdivision, the registrar issues a certificate for each lot, block, or parcel in the subdivision plan.

evidence.evidenceText: 18(5)Where the registrar is required pursuant to the provisions of this Act to register the title to land or to register land or to register a person as the owner of land or to register an instrument severing or consolidating land or a transfer, the registrar shall (a) cancel the certificate of registered ownership, if any, as to that land; and (b) issue to the owner, surviving owner, personal representative, agent or trustee, as the case may be, a certificate of registered ownership for that land and, in the case of a subdivision, a certificate of registered ownership for each lot, block or parcel in the subdivision plan.

objectives.objective: Recall the notice and statutory effect when certain titles are registered.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What notice must be issued for titles registered under specified orders or section 23, and what follows after that notice?
objectives.studyAnswer: When registering title under an order under section 12, 13, or 14, or title to previously unregistered land under section 23, the registrar shall issue and record under the Registry Act a prescribed-form notice. After that, the title is dealt with under the Land Titles Act, and the Act applies to every instrument or document relating to an interest in that land.

evidence.evidenceText: Where the registrar registers a title to land pursuant to an order under section 12, 13 or 14 or a title to previously unregistered land pursuant to section 23, the registrar shall issue and record under the Registry Act a notice in prescribed form and thereafter the title to the land shall be dealt with under this Act, and this Act applies to every instrument or document that relates to an interest in that land.

objectives.objective: Recall parcel identifier use in the title register.
objectives.guidedQuestion: How must a parcel be identified in the title register when its title is registered under the Act?
objectives.studyAnswer: Every parcel of land whose title is registered under the Act shall be identified in the title register by its approved parcel identifier.

evidence.evidenceText: Every parcel of land in respect of which a title is registered under this Act shall be identified by its approved parcel identifier in the title register.

title: Rejection records, amending instruments, and Registry Act documents
mainQuestion: What record, notice, amendment, and discretionary registration rules apply after rejection or for special instruments under section 18?
studySummary: When an instrument is rejected, the registrar records the rejection and reasons in the instrument record and notifies the presenter. The registrar cannot reject an instrument referred to in subsection 12(10), despite subsection 18(4). Instruments filed or registered under the Act may be amended by a prescribed-form amending instrument, subject to registrar-imposed terms and conditions. The Registrar General may order a proper registrar to register under the Land Titles Act a Registry Act document sufficient to pass an estate or interest in registered land, and once registered it has the same effect as if registered as an instrument.

objectives.objective: Recall what the registrar must do when rejecting an instrument.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What record and notice steps must follow rejection of an instrument?
objectives.studyAnswer: Upon rejecting an instrument, the registrar shall enter in the instrument record a record of the rejection and a memorandum of the reasons for rejection, and shall notify the person who presented the instrument for registration.

evidence.evidenceText: Upon the rejection of an instrument, the registrar shall enter in the instrument record a record of the rejection and a memorandum of the reasons for such rejection, and shall notify the person who presented the instrument for registration.

objectives.objective: Recall the subsection 12(10) exception to the rejection power.
objectives.guidedQuestion: Which instrument may the registrar not reject despite subsection 18(4)?
objectives.studyAnswer: Despite subsection 18(4), the registrar shall not reject an instrument referred to in subsection 12(10).

evidence.evidenceText: Notwithstanding subsection (4), the registrar shall not reject an instrument referred to in subsection 12(10).

objectives.objective: Recall how filed or registered instruments may be amended.
objectives.guidedQuestion: How may an instrument filed or registered under the Act be amended?
objectives.studyAnswer: It may be amended by filing or registering a prescribed-form amending instrument, subject to any terms and conditions the registrar imposes.

evidence.evidenceText: Any instrument that is filed or registered under this Act may, subject to such terms and conditions as the registrar may impose, be amended by the filing or registration of an amending instrument in prescribed form.

objectives.objective: Recall the Registrar General's discretionary order for certain Registry Act documents.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What may the Registrar General order for a Registry Act document dealing with land registered under the Land Titles Act?
objectives.studyAnswer: If a document sufficient to pass an estate or interest in land under the Registry Act deals with land registered under the Land Titles Act, the Registrar General may, in absolute discretion, order the proper registrar to register it under the Act; when so registered, it has the same effect as if registered as an instrument.

evidence.evidenceText: Notwithstanding anything in this Act, where a document sufficient to pass an estate or interest in land under the Registry Act deals with land registered under this Act, the Registrar General may, in his absolute discretion, order the proper registrar to register it under this Act, and when so registered it shall have the same effect as if registered as an instrument.

title: Unregistered instrument consequences for purchasers and judgment creditors
mainQuestion: When are unregistered instruments deemed fraudulent and void against subsequent purchasers or bona fide judgment creditors?
studySummary: Registry Act section 19 allows instruments to be registered in the registry office for the county where the lands lie. Subject to listed exceptions, an unregistered instrument is deemed fraudulent and void against later purchasers for valuable consideration whose conveyances are registered first. Also subject to those exceptions, an instrument not registered within three months after execution is deemed fraudulent and void against a bona fide judgment creditor when the judgment or memorial was registered before the conveyance was registered.

objectives.objective: Recall the consequence of non-registration against subsequent purchasers.
objectives.guidedQuestion: When is an unregistered instrument deemed fraudulent and void against a subsequent purchaser?
objectives.studyAnswer: Subject to subsections 19(3), 19(4), 19(4.1), and 19(5), an instrument not registered in the registry office for the county where the lands lie is deemed fraudulent and void against subsequent purchasers for valuable consideration whose conveyances are previously registered.

evidence.evidenceText: All instruments may be registered in the registry office for the county where the lands lie, and if not so registered, shall, subject to the provisions of subsections (3), (4), (4.1) and (5), be deemed fraudulent and void against subsequent purchasers for valuable consideration whose conveyances are previously registered.

objectives.objective: Recall the consequence of late registration against bona fide judgment creditors.
objectives.guidedQuestion: When is an instrument deemed fraudulent and void against a bona fide judgment creditor?
objectives.studyAnswer: Subject to subsections 19(3), 19(4), 19(4.1), and 19(5), an instrument not registered within three months of execution is deemed fraudulent and void against a bona fide judgment creditor when, before the registry of the conveyance, the judgment or a memorial of the judgment has been registered.

evidence.evidenceText: Subject to subsections (3), (4), (4.1) and (5), all instruments shall, if not registered within three months of the date of their execution, be deemed fraudulent and void as against any bona fide judgment creditor, when, prior to the registry of such conveyance, the judgment or a memorial of the judgment has been registered.
